tagline.text: Metro Manila's last mangroves and a haven for migratory birds

location.label: Location
location.text: Coast of Las Piñas and Parañaque, Metro Manila (Freedom Island and Long Island)

children.text: This coastal wetland reserve lies 30–60 minutes by car from central Manila. About 182 hectares of mangrove forest and mudflats make up a Ramsar wetland where migratory birds rest from August to April.

Las Piñas–Parañaque Wetland Park is a protected area off the coasts of Las Piñas and Parañaque in Metro Manila. Its official name is the Las Piñas–Parañaque Critical Habitat and Ecotourism Area (LPPCHEA), though most people now simply call it the Wetland Park. It covers about
181.63 hectares
, of which roughly
114 hectares
are tidal mudflats and several dozen hectares are mangrove forest. Its greatest appeal is the chance to see mudflats and mangroves in the middle of a huge city.

This land is not a natural island. The islands are artificial: they formed on dredged material and fill left after the Manila–Cavite Coastal Road and its reclamation work began in 1973, and the road opened in September 1985. In the years that followed, mangroves grew and birds gathered on their own. The two main islands are Freedom Island in Parañaque to the north and Long Island in Las Piñas to the south, plus one smaller island. There is a reason migratory birds stop here: broad mudflats are exposed around the islands, so food is plentiful. Mudflats, ponds and lagoons, salt marshes and mixed beach forest are packed into a small area, and it also serves as a spawning ground and nursery for fish.

Its protection status was raised step by step. It was declared a critical habitat by Presidential Proclamation No. 1412 in April 2007, listed as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention (site no. 2124) in March 2013, and made a national protected area under Republic Act No. 11038 (the E-NIPAS Act) in 2018. It is managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). On World Wetlands Day, February 2, 2024, the Wetland Center Museum opened, adding a visitor education function. Reports also say that construction of a Fisheries Learning Hub cum Mangrovetum and a watch tower next to the Wetland Center broke ground in December 2025. Whether it is finished and open should be checked locally.

It makes a good half-day outing for travelers. It suits anyone who wants to leave downtown Manila to see birds and mangroves, families who want a nature lesson with children, and photographers. However, opening hours and visiting procedures have differed over time, so be sure to check with the DENR regional office for Metro Manila or the park's official announcements before you go. The park is also a place where debate continues between development pressure and conservation. In February 2019 about 22 Manila Bay reclamation projects were announced, and critics said part of the wetland would be affected. In September 2025 the president vetoed a bill that would have added a 1,128-hectare buffer zone. At a Senate hearing in July 2026, the DENR reportedly said that the park's birds are not the cause of bird strikes at the airport and that a study pointed mainly to racing pigeons. Because of these developments, facilities and access may change, so check the latest news before visiting.
The park lies on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, so from August to April birds from China, Japan and Siberia feed on the mudflats. Up to about
5,000 birds
a day are said to be seen, with the Little Egret, Black-crowned Night Heron and Common Moorhen among the typical species.

Vulnerable species such as the Philippine Duck, a Philippine endemic, and the Chinese Egret are recorded here. The Philippine Duck is sometimes described as the only known breeding site in Metro Manila. Walking quietly with binoculars improves your chances of seeing them.

This is one of the few mangrove forests left in central Manila. Along the raised boardwalk, which keeps you off the roots, you can see mangroves known by local names such as Bungalon, Bakauan Babae and Nilad up close. The number of mangrove species is counted as either 11 or 23 depending on the source, and the forest area is given as 30–40 hectares in different sources.

The visitor hub, the Wetland Center, has the first wetland museum and an audio-visual room, so you can learn about the wetland's ecology and conservation before heading out. You can get an introduction to the park at the welcome space, The Wave.
Mudflats exposed at low tide are full of worms and shellfish, which draw the birds. In the late afternoon, when the sun sets over Manila Bay, the sky changes color and makes for good photos.
Inside the park is the Bambusetum, a botanical section with many bamboo species. It is a pleasant shady place to rest between wetland walks.

blocks.title: A fish nursery and fishers' livelihoods

children.text: The wetland also serves as a nursery where fish and shellfish grow, so it is tied to the livelihoods of nearby fishers. Coastal cleanups and mangrove planting events are held regularly.

Mangroves reduce coastal erosion, soften storm surges and ease flooding. They also improve water quality and store carbon. Walking through the wetland, you can see for yourself how this kind of nature protects a city on the coast.
Leave your hotel. From central Manila it takes about
30–60 minutes
toward the Coastal Road, and traffic is heavy at rush hour, so start early.
Arrive at the visitor area, check registration and instructions, and hear the park introduction at The Wave.
Visit the wetland museum in the Wetland Center. Learning about the birds and mangroves first makes the walk afterward much more enjoyable.
Walk slowly along the boardwalk. Birds are sensitive to noise, so keep your voice low and scan the mudflats with binoculars.
Rest in the Bambusetum, then pack up and leave. Have lunch along the Coastal Road or at SM Mall of Asia.
The best times are early morning and late afternoon in the migratory season (August–April). Timing your visit for low tide, when the mudflats are exposed, lets you see more birds.
Finish lunch and a rest at SM Mall of Asia or by Manila Bay, then head to the park.
Get your instructions at the visitor area and walk the boardwalk section.
Take photos as the western sky turns red. It is safer to leave the park before sunset.
Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) is close to the park in straight-line distance, but roads can be congested, so allow
30–60 minutes
Ride-hailing taxis such as Grab are convenient from the airport. Fares vary by time of day, so check in the app.
There is some walking inside the park, so leave your luggage at your hotel.

items.title: By public transport from central Manila

children.text: From central Manila, you can take a jeepney or bus toward Roxas Boulevard and the Coastal Road and get off near the park entrance.
Local jeepney routes (for example, the Alabang–Baclaran Coastal Road route) run along the coastal road. Confirm the exact drop-off point locally.
The last stretch is often done by tricycle or on foot.
Use the entrance on the Coastal Road (Manila–Cavite Expressway) side, close to the Parañaque–Las Piñas boundary.
Parking availability varies over time, so check beforehand.
The best time is the migratory season, August to April. November to February is especially comfortable, with relatively cool weather for walking.
Early morning and late afternoon are best in the day. At midday there is little shade and it is very hot. Mudflats are exposed at low tide, when the most birds gather.
In 2019 heavy rain lowered oxygen levels and caused a fish kill. In the rainy season, water conditions and whether you can visit may change, so check the weather.

There is little large-scale lodging near the park, so most visitors stay in central Manila or at hotels around Pasay and SM Mall of Asia and travel from there. The Mall of Asia and Manila Bay area has many hotels and restaurants, so it is easy to combine with a park visit. Around Mall of Asia you can take care of dinner and shopping in one place, so visiting the wetland in the morning and the mall in the afternoon works well. Rooms come at a range of prices, so compare them on a booking app.

There is no large restaurant inside the park. Bring water, light snacks, a hat and sunscreen, and have lunch at a restaurant along the Coastal Road or at a mall. You must take your trash out with you.
Before you go, check opening hours and visiting procedures with the DENR regional office for Metro Manila or the park's official announcements.
Go in the early morning or late afternoon. The sun is strong at midday.
Be sure to bring binoculars, a hat, sunscreen, insect repellent and water.
Walk quietly on the boardwalk so you do not startle the birds.
Wear comfortable sneakers. The ground can be wet or muddy.
Time your visit for the migratory season, August–April, and there is far more to see.
Rather than relying on a Grab for the round trip, think ahead about how you will get back.
The park is also home to migratory birds and a livelihood for fishers. If you want to photograph fishers or children, ask first.
Volunteer coastal cleanups are held regularly, so if you are interested, look for the schedule through the DENR or park announcements.
This is a protected area, so stay on permitted zones and paths and do not touch the birds or mangroves. Visiting procedures may change.
Pets and littering are prohibited at many sites like this. Follow the instructions.
There are many mosquitoes around the wetland, and paths are slippery when it rains.

Nearby reclamation projects and park-related bills (such as the veto of the buffer zone bill) remain controversial, so facilities and access may change. Illegal dumping, plastic pollution and water pollution are also problems for this wetland, so be sure to take your trash with you.
Do not go alone into remote areas, and leave before sunset.
Keep your belongings out of sight. The usual precautions for Metro Manila apply.
A church on the same southern Manila coast with a bamboo pipe organ dating from around 1824. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so check locally.
A large shopping mall on the Manila Bay side, good for continuing with a meal and a sunset stroll. Travel time varies greatly with traffic.
The bay the wetland park faces, famous for its sunsets.
An aquarium and marine park that is good for children and easy to combine with a Manila Bay itinerary.
